The appellant was appointed senior jailor, Surendranagar District Jail, and was appointed senior police officer in the Gondal State. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the High Court erred in fastening the liability in respect of the arrears of pay on the State of Maharashtra. The High court held that the appellant was entitled to the decree for arrears of salary and the State of Bombay was entitled to recover the arrears of salary from the appellant. The High, Court held that there was a breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution. The High. Court held that it was not a case of a breach of contract. The High 'Court further held that the decree of the High Court was illegal and invalid. The High was therefore right in holding that there was no breach of article 310(2) and that the decree was void. The High appeal by special leave was dismissed. Held, that the High court erred in fastating the liability in the facts of the case. The High "Court erred in fasting the liability in favour of the appellant. It was not correct to say that the decree passed by the High Court could not be varied so as to show that the appellant had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners, maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The decree of the trial court was not a decree for the payment of arrears of salary. The decree was not a nullity. The decree passed by a High Court was not a mere decree for payment of salary. It was a decree for payment to the appellant. In the present case the decree was not executed by the appellant. There was no contract between the appellant and the respondent. The decree did not contain any express provision for a power to dismiss at pleasure. The decree only provided for a power of dismissal. The decree not only was a decree but also a decree for arrears. The decree more properly falls under section 61. The decree is not a decree but only a decree for recovery of salary. In the instant case the decree did not specify the period of the decree. The decree in question was not a judgment and decree for recovery. The decree for arrears was not a part of the decree and the decree for recovery was not a final decree. The High Courts were not bound to follow the decree in the absence of any express provision in the decree.

The respondent, a Custodian of Evacuee Property, who was a Custodian of evacuee property, was given a notice to the appellants, and the appellants, on the terms of the section, to the Custodian, and the Custodian, on the other hand, issued a notice to them, Exhibit C, stating that the appellants had no authority to sell the mills and the factory to them in certain circumstances. The appellants, however, filed a writ petition in the High Court, challenging the validity of the notice, and the High Court 's order, dated the 31st day of March 1954, in so far as it related to the lease of the mills and, in particular, the lease granted in favour of the appellants, was illegal. The High Court held that the lease was not void and that the respondent was not entitled to the protection of the section. Held, that the section was not a mere piece of legislation and that the section did not by implication repeal statutes conferring rights on lessees, and that the power could not be exercised "notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force". The section merely provided that the lease might be cancelled or varied by the Custodian, but it was not open to the appellants to contend that the lease could be cancelled or modified by the Custodian. The section merely provides that the lease may be cancelled or altered by the Custodian or by the Custodian in the circumstances of the case. The section does not by implication expressly empower the Custodian to cancel the lease. The section is not intended to repel a possible contention that the lease should be cancelled or changed by the Custodian and that it must be held that the power cannot be exercised " notwithstanding anything contained in the other law for time being in operation". The section does so expressly empower the custodian to vary the terms of a lease, and that power cannot be abridged by reference to the provision that it could be exercised "subject to the conditions that it could not be done" in the present case.

The appellant was a public temple at Amalner. The sansthan had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and the average gross annual income was Rs. 11,000/ . After the passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, the State Government issued a notification under section 18 of that Act on the basis of the provisions of the Act. The appellant was a trustee of the temple. The appellant filed an application under section 72 of the Act to the District Judge of West Khandesh at Dhulia for a declaration that the Sansthan was a public trust within the meaning of section 2(13) of the Act and that the Sansthan had no right to the temple. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the temple was a private temple and not a public temple. Held, that the temple is a private temple. The temple is a public temple and not an institution of public nature. The temple was a public religious endowment. The temple in its own name was a public endowment. The deity was installed only under special circumstances with special permission. The temple could not be said to be a public temple within the meaning ofs. 2(13). The temple was not a public religious temple. The deity installed in the temple was not merely the accredited daily)..... but also the multitude of the public who go to the temple for Darshan of the deity and for offerings. The deity in the temple in its present name was the sole trustee of the deity. The temple, in its own hand, was a public institution. The temple had no right of worship. The temple did not have special permission for the worship of the deity but only the institution of the temple for the purpose of maintenance of the worship. The deity, in its present form, was not merely an institution of a public nature. It was not a private temple, but was a public public temple. The public temple was not an institution for public purposes. The temple itself was not a religious temple. In view of the penal provision under section 18(1) of the , the temple was an institution of the public character. The temple being a public temple, the temple was in the public interest. The temple must be a public religious institution. The deity must be a private temple within the definition of section 2 (13) of section 2 of the Act, and the temple must be held to be a private institution. The public is not merely the institution of public worship but also the institution of a private temple in favour of the temple or of the Sansthan for the purpose for which it is created. The temple cannot be held to have any public interest.

The appellant was a tenant of a part of a building in the State of Madras. The lease was granted by the State Government to the appellant on January 10, 1942, and the lease was granted to him on September 7, 1949. The lease continued to be in force till February 1, 1947, and the appellant was granted a lease for a period of 20 years commencing from February 1,1942, and ending on November 30, 1947. The lease however was granted on September 7. 1949, and the lessee was granted a mining lease for a short period commencing from February 1942, but the lease was renewed on September 7 and the lease expired on September 7, 1949. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease. The Collector rejected the application. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the lease was not valid and that the lease could not be terminated without any compensation under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The High court held that the appellant was entitled to the grant of the lease on the expiry of the fifth year to the appellant. The High, Court held that it was not necessary to consider whether the right of the appellant to terminate the lease was a right or not. The High. Court held that there was no valid and valid lease for the period of 20 to 30 years commencing from the date of the lease and that the appellant had no right to terminate the tenancy. The High 'Court further held that the right of a lessee to terminate the leases was not a right or privilege under the second Proviso to section 20 of the Abolition of the Act. The appellant contended that the right to terminate a lease was not a vested right and that the right was not a mere right and that it was a right conferred on the Government to terminate the rights created after July 1, 1945. Held, that the appellant could not terminate the lease without any compensation. The mere fact that the lease itself was determined under the second provisos to section 20, would not make the right created after July I, 1945, for a period exceeding one year. The second proviso to the section makes no difference. The second condition is that the term of the lease should be renewed at the option of the lessee for one period not exceeding the duration of the original lease. The second clause in the section provides that the term shall be renewed at a time and the lessee shall be entitled to the lease only for a period not exceeding one year and shall be entitled at the end of the period of the original leases. The second sub section also makes the right created before July 1, 1955, void as against the Government. The second Proviso to the section provides for the termination of the lease by the Government.
